hints: Think about what you actually see when limewater goes milky, a white solid forming from ions already in solution plus the gas bubbled in.
walkthrough:
Picture the milky change**
You start with a clear, colourless solution of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$. When you bubble in $\text{CO}_2$, it turns milky white. That milkiness is tiny solid particles of $\text{CaCO}_3$ suspended in water, with water also formed as the other product.

Balance the atoms**
Put the four species together: $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ plus $\text{CO}_2$ giving $\text{CaCO}_3$ plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Check: one Ca, one C, four O and two H on each side, so it is already balanced as $\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{CO}_2 \longrightarrow \text{CaCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

hints: For this test to work you need two things, enough dissolved hydroxide to react with the gas, and a carbonate product you can actually see.
walkthrough:
Recall what makes the test visible**
Limewater works because dissolved $\text{OH}^-$ reacts with $\text{CO}_2$ to make $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, and then $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ plus $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ gives insoluble white $\text{CaCO}_3$. Any replacement must do the same job.

Apply this to barium**
Like $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$, $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is soluble enough to provide a clear alkaline solution containing $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^-$. Its carbonate, $\text{BaCO}_3$, is insoluble, so bubbling $\text{CO}_2$ gives the same milky white precipitate: $\text{Ba(OH)}_2 + \text{CO}_2 \longrightarrow \text{BaCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Final answer: $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is sufficiently soluble to give $\text{OH}^-$ in solution and $\text{BaCO}_3$ is insoluble, so a white precipitate forms with $\text{CO}_2$.

hints: Compare solubility down Group 2, hydroxides become more soluble from Mg to Ba, so think how concentrated a saturated $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ solution can be.
Even if a little carbonate ion forms, ask whether magnesium carbonate would appear as a solid precipitate.
walkthrough:
See why almost no reagent is present**
Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group. $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is essentially insoluble, so a saturated solution contains only a trace of dissolved $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^-$. There is hardly any alkali to react with $\text{CO}_2$.

See why no milkiness appears**
For calcium and barium the carbonates $\text{CaCO}_3$ and $\text{BaCO}_3$ are insoluble, giving the white ppt. By contrast $\text{MgCO}_3$ is soluble in water, so even the small amount formed stays in solution. With no precipitate, there is no visible test, so $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ cannot be used.

Final answer: $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is insoluble / sparingly soluble so saturated solution contains very little $\text{OH}^-$.
$\text{MgCO}_3$ is soluble so no white precipitate is seen.

hints: State the observed stability order first, which carbonate needs the highest temperature to decompose, $\text{MgCO}_3$ or $\text{BaCO}_3$?
Link decomposition to the $\text{M}^{2+}$ ion, how does ionic radius change from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$?
Think about how a small, highly charging cation distorts the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion and weakens a C-O bond to release $\text{CO}_2$ more easily.
walkthrough:
Describe the trend**
Heating $\text{MCO}_3 \longrightarrow \text{MO} + \text{CO}_2$ needs a much higher temperature as you go from Mg to Ca to Sr to Ba. So thermal stability increases down Group 2. $\text{MgCO}_3$ decomposes on gentle heating while $\text{BaCO}_3$ needs strong heating.

Connect to cation size**
All these cations are $2+$, but ionic radius increases down the group: $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is small, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is large. Charge density therefore falls. A small $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is strongly polarising, a large $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is weakly polarising.

Explain polarisation of carbonate**
Picture $\text{M}^{2+}$ pulling on the electron cloud of the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion. A small cation distorts the carbonate strongly, weakening one C-O bond and making it easier to break to form $\text{CO}_2$ plus $\text{O}^{2-}$ in the oxide. Down the group, larger cations cause less distortion of $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, the carbonate ion is more stable, so decomposition temperature rises.

Final answer: Carbonates become more thermally stable down Group 2, $\text{MgCO}_3$ decomposes most easily, $\text{BaCO}_3$ is most stable.
Down the group cation radius / size increases.
Larger cation has lower charge density and polarises / distorts the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion less, so the C-O bond is less weakened and more heat is needed to decompose.

hints: Look up the ionic radii of $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ in the Data Booklet and compare their sizes.
Apply the same polarisation argument as for Group 2, which ion will distort $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ more strongly?
walkthrough:
Pull out the data**
From the Data Booklet, $r(\text{Ni}^{2+}) = 0.070\,\text{nm}$ and $r(\text{Ca}^{2+}) = 0.099\,\text{nm}$. Both ions carry the same $2+$ charge, so size alone controls polarising power. $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ is significantly smaller.

Predict relative stability**
Smaller $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ has higher charge density, so it distorts the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ electron cloud more than $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ does. That weakens the carbonate ion further toward $\text{NiO} + \text{CO}_2$. Therefore $\text{NiCO}_3$ is less thermally stable and decomposes more readily than $\text{CaCO}_3$.

Final answer: Radius of $\text{Ni}^{2+} = 0.070\,\text{nm}$ is smaller than radius of $\text{Ca}^{2+} = 0.099\,\text{nm}$.
$\text{Ni}^{2+}$ polarises $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ more strongly, so $\text{NiCO}_3$ decomposes more readily / at lower temperature than $\text{CaCO}_3$.
